data.content_ref: inline:The target's claim that the preference for corroborated theories is 'defensible only as a constitutive rule of the scientific game' rests on a false dilemma that misrepresents Popper's actual position. Popper explicitly rejected conventionalism — the view that methodological rules are mere conventions of a 'game' — and grounded the preference in the regulative ideal of truth (via Tarski's correspondence theory) and the notion of verisimilitude: we prefer corroborated theories because they have survived severer tests and are, rationally, closer to the truth. By asserting the preference is 'defensible only' as a constitutive rule with 'no deeper logical ground than the desire to play the game,' the target collapses Popper into the very conventionalism Popper argued against, and simultaneously undercuts its own claim: if the commitment rests on nothing but the desire to play, there is no rational basis to prefer the scientific game over astrology or pseudoscience, whose practitioners also desire to play their games. The target's own counterconditions gesture at this vulnerability but never resolve it, leaving the argument internally self-undermining.
